 EU agency warns websites may need to be taken offline as PHP prepares patches for vulnerabilities
 Updated / Wednesday, 21 Oct 2026
 11:44
 Getty
 PHP programming language used across large parts of the internet 
 The developers of the widely used PHP programming language said they would release patches for two critical vulnerabilities, as EU cybersecurity officials warned organisations unable to apply the fixes should take affected websites offline.
 PHP is used across large parts of the internet, and speculation has circulated over the past day that websites running the software could be exposed to serious cyber intrusions.
 "PHP is everywhere. It quietly powers WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento ‌sites, shared hosting platforms, control panels, and ⁠an awful lot of software that doesn't even advertise that it runs PHP under the hood," cybersecurity company Huntress said in a blog post.
 In a security update, PHP said both vulnerabilities were rated 9.2 on the CVSS v4.0 severity scale and urged users to "upgrade as soon as the release is available".
 It said a patch for both vulnerabilities ‌was scheduled for 2pm.
 The European Union Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-EU) said yesterday in an advisory that the 9.2 rating indicated a ⁠risk of unauthenticated remote code execution, a type of flaw that can allow attackers to run ‌malicious code on vulnerable systems without logging in.
 CERT-EU urged organisations to prepare for the ⁠immediate patching of affected ‌assets and said those unable to do so should consider taking affected sites offline.
 The Australian Cyber Security Centre (ACSC) issued similar guidance, urging organisations to identify PHP systems in their environments, prepare to apply patches and monitor applications for signs of malicious activity.
 "ACSC ⁠is currently not aware of active exploitation related to these vulnerabilities," the agency said.
 Web hosting provider GoDaddy said ⁠the flaws could allow attackers to execute code on affected servers over the internet, potentially leading to data theft, website defacement or full system compromise.
 PHP's security team said details of the vulnerabilities, affected versions and the fixed releases would be published when patches are issued.
 CERT-EU and the ACSC said all PHP versions from PHP 5 onward could be affected, although PHP has not disclosed which versions are vulnerable.
